course_description:
CRIM7000 provides an overview of the major approaches to understanding criminal behaviour, and how these approaches help us understand and respond to particular crime problems. This course focusses on issues such as: What is criminology? What is crime? How much crime is there in Australia? Who is at most risk of being a victim of crime? How do we measure crime? What are the major approaches to explaining crime? What can inhibit criminal behaviour? How does participation in crime change over the life-course? How might criminological knowledge impact the prevention of crime and the development of crime and justice policies? This course is designed to broadly survey how we study criminal behaviour, provide insights into different issues studied in criminology, and prepare students (by introducing foundational concepts) for more advanced study in cybercrime.

course_aims: The aim of this course is to provide students with an overview of the nature of crimeﾠin Australian and international contexts.ﾠ It will provide a thorough grounding in the various criminological approaches to understanding the causes of criminal behaviour and will examine the major methods for measuring crime, as well as the dominant theoretical perspectives in the field of Criminology.

learning_outcomes.description: Explain foundational concepts and theories in criminology: Explain key criminological concepts, definitions, and major theoretical perspectives used to understand criminal behaviour in relation to cybercrime and cybersecurity.
Construct evidence-based criminological arguments: Develop clear, structured, and academically informed arguments supported by relevant research and data.

Find and synthesise criminological information: Locate, evaluate, and integrate information from diverse sources, including academic research, crime data, and media to inform criminological analysis of cybercrime and cybersecurity.

Apply ethical approaches to criminological research and cybersecurity practice: Identify and critically assess ethical issues in criminological research and professional practice, including responsible use of AI and emerging technologies.

Demonstrate cultural competency in criminology: Recognise and appreciate how social diversity, inequality, and cultural contexts shape criminal behaviour, the cybersecurity environment, and justice system responses.

assessment_details.title: Cybercrime Fact Checking Investigation
assessment_details.other_conditions: AI Required. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Due Date: Wednesday September 2nd 2026, 4pm (Week 6) Word count: 1500 words (+/- 10%) To complete Assessment 1 (Cybercrime Fact Checking Investigation) and Assessment 3 (Theory Application Argument), you must choose a real cybercrime incident or criminal case involving cybercrime. You can find information in the Assessment folder on Blackboard Ultra on how to choose your cybercrime incident. Why have I assigned this assessment: Information in the 21st century is distributed and collected in a variety of ways. Being able to understand and judge the reliability and validity of data has never been more essential, particularly given that every person possess their own biases and these biases are reflected by machine learning. AI literacy is essential in modern criminology because artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in policing, courts, and corrections - often with profound implications for justice and equity. Cyber Master's students need to understand and recognise how AI systems can reproduce bias, how to verify AI-generated information, and how to evaluate algorithmic decision-making critically. This is not just about using technology; it is about understanding how technology shapes crime, justice, and inequality. By developing AI literacy, students gain the analytical tools to work effectively in AI-mediated criminal justice systems while maintaining their commitment to fairness, accountability, and human dignity. PART 1: Select your crime case/incident Choose one cybercrime incident that has generated public discussion. This could be: A specific cybercrime case focusing on an individual (e.g., cyberstalking and harassment case, identity theft case, fraud case, etc.) A specific cybercrime incident that involves more than one offender (e.g., ransomware attacks, malware infections, phishing, DDoS, data breaches, etc.) A specific cybercrime case that involves institutional wrongdoing (e.g., cyber warfare, infrastructure sabotage, cyber espionage, disinformation campaign, etc.) Requirements: Must be from a credible news source (e.g., ABC News, The Guardian, BBC, local newspapers, etc.) Must include a link to your news article in your submission May include cybercrime cases that have not been finalised May include unsolved cybercriminal cases May include international incidents Provide in your submission: Case Name Category/Classification of the Case Link to your news article PART 2: AI-Generated Summaries Use two different AI tools/platforms (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot, Gemini, etc.) to generate summaries of your chosen cybercrime incident. Prompt each AI with: "Provide a detailed summary of [cybercrime incident name/description] including what happened, who was involved, the criminal charges or outcomes, and any key facts about the case." For each AI tool/platform, document: Which AI tool you used The exact prompt you used Screenshot or copy of the AI's complete response Provide an analysis of the outputs. In your response, compare what each AI stated. Consider the following: How did the two AI summaries differ? How are they similar? Which seemed more detailed or accurate at first glance? Which output feels more accurate? Why? PART 3: Fact-Checking Claims Now become a fact-checker! Select four claims from across the AI summaries and verify the selected claims. Identify and fact-check at least 4 specific claims the AI made. For each claim include: The Claim (quote exactly what the AI said) Verification Decision: TRUE - Accurate✓ ⚠️ PARTIALLY TRUE - Mostly accurate but missing nuance/context ✗ FALSE - Incorrect or misleading ? UNVERIFIABLE - Cannot confirm with available sources 3. Evidence: What sources did you use to verify? (Provide the links/citations you relied on in making your decision) What did you find (True, partially true, false, or unverifiable)? If the claim was false/misleading, provide the accurate information about this claim. Why might the AI have gotten this wrong? If the claim was true, why might the AI have been able to accurately provide this information? PART 4: Critical Reflection Write a reflection and consider: · AI accuracy · Implications for research/industry · Your own assumptions/process/learning/reflections Please see the task sheet on Blackboard for additional details. Please note that reproductions of AI output do not count towards the total word count. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Translation (MT) are emerging tools that may support students in completing this assessment task. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference any use of AI or MT in each instance. A failure to reference AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Additional resources are available through UQ AI Student Hub . assessment_details.task_description: Due Date: To be submitted at the end of the associated tutorial Weighting: 40% Tutorials in CRIM7000 are designed to do two things: Firstly, the exercises provide important information and direction in completing your assessments. Secondly, these exercises help you practice and develop the theory application and argument skills learned in the lecture and reading material each week. During tutorials in Weeks 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, and 12, you will complete an interactive exercise. These exercises are based on analysing and responding to real-world crime scenarios presented through videos, case studies, artifacts, or news reports shown in class. You will work through these scenarios by applying criminological theories and concepts to explain criminal behaviour, identify contributing factors, and provide analytical responses. These exercises are designed to help you practice critical thinking skills, engage with real-world crime scenarios, and demonstrate your understanding of lecture content and reading material through practical application. Explicit instructions on how each exercise works will be provided at the beginning of each tutorial. Assessment Security Requirements: These are secure, identity-verified assessments with the following requirements: · In-person attendance mandatory - Exercises can only be completed during your assigned tutorial. · No digital devices permitted - Computers, phones, tablets, or other digital devices cannot be used during the exercise – unless stated otherwise. · Paper-based responses only - You must complete responses on the paper materials provided by your tutor. · No external materials - Textbooks, notes, or outside materials are not permitted during the exercise. · No AI assistance - Artificial intelligence tools cannot be used to assist or complete these exercises. · Translation - Translation dictionaries are the only outside materials allowed. Failure to abide by these conditions may result in an academic misconduct allegation. Grading Structure: There are 8 exercises offered over the course of the semester. You may attempt all of them; however, your best 5 exercise scores will contribute to 40% of your final grade. Each exercise is worth 8 points (Total possible: 40 points toward final grade). Everything you need to complete each exercise will be provided to you in class. Why does this assessment matter? These interactive exercises are designed to help you apply theoretical knowledge to real-world crime scenarios in a supervised setting. They are designed to ensure that you are meeting the learning outcomes of this course and developing skills including critical thinking. This assessment gives you an opportunity to demonstrate what you have learned and build up confidence in theory application before your major assessment. In addition, these exercises help you practice exam-style thinking in a low-stakes environment while ensuring the academic integrity of your learning. Marking criteria: Criteria including rubrics are available in the ‘Assessments’ folder on the course Blackboard site. AI Use: This assessment task will be completed in-person. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempted use of AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct Policy. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.title: Theory Application Argument
assessment_details.task_description: Due Date: Monday November 9th 2026, 4pm (Exam Week 1) Word Count: 1500 words (+/- 10%) HURDLE REQUIREMENT: You must submit a completed Generative AI Usage Statement (template provided in Blackboard). Even if you did not use AI to support your writing, you must still submit a completed Generative AI Usage Statement. Failure to do so will result in a grade of 0 for this assessment. You will apply ONE criminological theory to explain the criminal behaviour in your chosen cybercrime case (from the Cybercrime Fact Checking Investigation assessment). Your submission includes TWO components: (1) a focused written argument explaining how your theory applies to the cybercrime case, and (2) a visual pathway diagram mapping the theoretical explanation into the specific facts of the case. Why have I assigned this task? Criminologists use theory to explain why crime occurs and why people offend. This assessment asks you to apply a theoretical framework to understand and explain a real world cybercrime incident or criminal behaviour which utilised the internet (cyber-enabled crime or cyber-dependent crime). The written component develops your ability to effectively construct an evidence-based argument, while the visual diagram helps you see and communicate the causal pathways that the theory proposes. Together, these skills are essential for anyone pursuing advanced criminological study and/or a career in cybersecurity. Task Description: Part A: Written Component (1500 words - 25 marks) Your written argument must answer the following question: How does [insert chosen theory here] explain why [insert chosen offender here] engaged in [insert cyber-related criminal behaviour here]? OR How does [insert chosen theory here] explain how [insert chosen cyber incident here] occurred? Your written argument should include: - A theory covered in the course and contained in the list provided on Blackboard - An explanation of the central principles or key elements of the theory and how these principles/elements come together in forming a criminal pathway - ONE example from peer-reviewed literature demonstrating where your chosen theory has been used in explaining similar cases/types of cybercrime - An argument as to how your chosen theory explains the criminal behaviour in your chosen cybercrime case - ONE critique of your chosen theory that is supported by evidence and peer-reviewed literature This is not a formal essay so there is no need for an introduction or conclusion. Just focus on your argument. PART B: Theory Pathway Diagram (15 marks) On one A4 page, you will create a visual diagram of the causal pathway you are arguing is occurring to produce the criminal behaviour in your cybercrime incident. Examples of how to do this will be provided in lecture and in tutorials. You may draw this pathway by hand (as long as it can be clearly read) or digitally create the diagram pathway. Your diagram must visually demonstrate HOW your case maps onto the causal pathway proposed by your chosen theory. You must include examples/evidence from your chosen cybercrime case on the theoretical diagram. Source Requirements: A minimum of 6 scholarly, peer-reviewed references Reliable sources about your chosen cybercrime case (i.e. news reports, court documents, official reports, etc.) Technical Requirements: You may use AI to SUPPORT your writing. Tutorials will include a discussion of what appropriate AI usage looks like for this assessment. This course prepares you to be able to have ethical and responsible conversations about the use of AI and also develop ethical practices when using AI. The Generative AI Use Statement is linked to this component of the class. Please note that you must submit a completed AI Use Statement regardless of whether you have used AI. Failure to do so will result in a 0 grade for this assessment. The visual diagram, reference list, and AI statement are not included in the word count. Please see the task sheet on Blackboard for additional details. Read full task description Hide full task description
